results.title: Sensitivity Analysis and Bounds (Chapter 22) - Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences
results.content: In Part V we study methods that confront the unconfoundedness assumption. In Chapter 21 we discussed methods to assess the plausibility of this assumption by combining it with additional assumptions. In the current chapter we relax the unconfoundedness assumption without replacing it with additional assumptions, and so do not focus on obtaining point estimates of the causal estimands of interest. This bounds or partial identification approach, as it is called, leads to sharp results, but at the same time will be seen to limit severely the types of inferences about causal effects that can be drawn from observational data. If we allow for large violations in the Rosenbaum-Rubin approach, it will often lead to essentially the same results as the Manski bounds approach, but with limited violations of the unconfoundedness assumption, the sensitivity approach results in narrower ranges for the estimands than the partial identification approach. # Save book to Kindle.

results.title: Weak instruments and identification | Causal Inference Class Notes
results.content:
Title: Weak instruments and identification | Causal Inference Class Notes
Weak instruments can lead to biased and inconsistent estimates in instrumental variable analysis. The notes also cover partial identification, bounds on parameters, and alternative methods for estimating causal effects when weak instruments are a concern. * Weak instruments are a common challenge in instrumental variable (IV) estimation, arising when the correlation between the instrument and the endogenous regressor is low. * Weak instruments can lead to biased and inconsistent estimates, as well as unreliable hypothesis tests and confidence intervals. * Identifying and addressing weak instruments is crucial for obtaining valid causal estimates in IV analysis. * Weak instruments can lead to inconsistent IV estimators, meaning that the estimator does not converge to the true parameter value as the sample size increases. * The inconsistency of IV estimators with weak instruments arises because the correlation between the instrument and the endogenous regressor does not increase sufficiently with the sample size. * Stock and Yogo (2005) developed critical values for the Cragg-Donald statistic that allow researchers to test for weak instruments based on the maximum acceptable bias or size distortion of the IV estimator. * Weak instruments can distort the size and power of hypothesis tests in IV estimation. * Weak instruments can lead to invalid and misleading confidence intervals for the IV estimator. * Implementing appropriate strategies can help researchers obtain more reliable causal estimates in the presence of weak instruments. * Weak instruments and irrelevant instruments are two distinct problems in IV estimation, with different implications for inference. * Weak instruments can pose challenges for identification in IV models, as the causal effect of interest may not be point-identified. * With weak instruments, the IV estimator may not converge to a single point, but it can still provide information about the set of parameter values consistent with the data and assumptions. * Partial identification methods, such as set estimation and moment inequality approaches, can be used to construct bounds on the causal effect in the presence of weak instruments. * When weak instruments are a concern, researchers may consider alternative methods for estimating causal effects that do not rely on instrumental variables.

Title: 7. Assessing Bias in the Estimation of Causal Effects: Rosenbaum Bounds on Matching Estimators and Instrumental Variables Estimation with Imperfect Instruments | CiNii Research
* 【Updated on January 20, 2026】 Integration of CiNii Books into CiNii Research. * Trial version of CiNii Research Knowledge Graph Search feature is available on CiNii Labs. * 【Updated on November 26, 2025】Regarding the recording of “Research Data” and “Evidence Data”. * Incorporated Jxiv preprints from JaLC and adding coverage from NDL Search. Assessing Bias in the Estimation of Causal Effects: Rosenbaum Bounds on Matching Estimators and Instrumental Variables Estimation with Imperfect Instruments. DOI   Web Site  3 Citations. :   Social Science Centre Berlin (WZB). ## Bibliographic Information. :   * https://journals.sagepub.com/page/policies/text-and-data-mining-license. :   * 10.1111/j.0081-1750.2004.00154.x. ## Search this article. Propensity score matching provides an estimate of the effect of a “treatment” variable on an outcome variable that is largely free of bias arising from an association between treatment status and observable variables. However, matching methods are not robust against “hidden bias” arising from unobserved variables that simultaneously affect assignment to treatment and the outcome variable. One strategy for addressing this problem is the Rosenbaum bounds approach, which allows the analyst to determine how strongly an unmeasured confounding variable must affect selection into treatment in order to undermine the conclusions about causal effects from a matching analysis. Instrumental variables (IV) estimation provides an alternative strategy for the estimation of causal effects, but the method typically reduces the precision of the estimate and has an additional source of uncertainty that derives from the untestable nature of the assumptions of the IV approach. A method of assessing this additional uncertainty is proposed so that the total uncertainty of the IV approach can be comparedwith the Rosenbaum bounds approach to uncertainty using matching methods. Because the approaches rely on different information and different assumptions, they provide complementary information about causal relationships. The approach is illustrated via an analysis of the impact of unemployment insurance on the timing of reemployment, the postunemployment wage, and the probability of relocation, using data from several panels of the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP). ## Journal. ## Citations (3)\*help. ## Report a problem. results.title: [PDF] Sharp Bounds for Generalized Causal Sensitivity Analysis
results.content: In the special case of a single binary treatment, our bounds for (condi-tional) average treatment effects coincide with recent optimality results for causal sensitivity analysis. As a result, we obtain sharp bounds for various causal effects, including (conditional) average treatment effects but also effects for mediation analysis and path analysis (see Fig. 1) and for distributional effects, which have not been studied under an MSM-type sensitivity analysis previously. Furthermore, MSM-based causal sensitivity analysis is restricted to (conditional) average treatment effects and is thus not applicable for complex settings such as effects for mediation analysis and path analysis or distributional effects. If all confounders between treatment and mediators and outcome were observed, we could (under additional assumptions) identify the causal effect Q(x, ¯ aℓ+1, M) from the observational distribution PV on V by replacing all do-operations with conditional probabilities according to the backdoor criterion [55]. However, under unobserved confounding, identifiability is not possible because SCMs M and M′ exist, which induce the same observational distribution PV, but which result in different causal effects Q(x, ¯ aℓ+1, M) ̸= Q(x, ¯ aℓ+1, M′) [54, 74]. 3.2 Causal sensitivity analysis In the following, we formalize causal sensitivity analysis as maximizing/minimizing the causal effect Q(x, ¯ aℓ+1, M) over all SCMs M that are compatible with a predefined sensitivity model. However, a sensitivity model must additionally restrict the joint distribution of both observed and unobserved variables in order to allow for informative bounds on the causal effect.
